finding.claim: The /mirror endpoint checks the host with endswith('example.com') (no leading dot), so attacker-controlled hosts such as evil-example.com or attackerexample.com pass. The server then fetches the URL. The check does not constrain scheme or port, and httpx does not follow redirects by default (httpx 0.20+), so redirects are not an extra bypass. Userinfo tricks do not help because hostname is parsed the same way. The unused ALLOWED_SUFFIX constant has a leading dot, which suggests the dotted form was intended. An attacker registers a domain like attackerexample.com that resolves to 169.254.169.254 or 127.0.0.1 (or serves content there), so the server makes requests to internal services. Only the response length is returned, which limits data exfiltration to a blind or oracle style, but internal requests are still made.

trace.note: url taken from the query string
weak suffix check host.endswith('example.com'), no dot boundary, no scheme/port/IP validation
the original unparsed url is fetched by httpx; the response length is returned

finding.guards_checked: Only the endswith('example.com') hostname check. It lacks a dot boundary, so evil-example.com passes. There is no scheme restriction (http/https only is enforced by httpx anyway), no private-IP or DNS-resolution check, and no DNS pinning. The ALLOWED_SUFFIX constant is unused. The fetched value is the raw url, not the parsed one. httpx does not follow redirects by default.

verdict.guard_found: Only host.endswith('example.com') at mirror.py:13 (suffix check, no dot boundary); no middleware, auth, scheme, or IP checks exist; the file is the only one in the directory.
verdict.reason: The `url` query parameter (mirror.py:11) is attacker-controlled, and the only guard is the non-closing `endswith('example.com')` at mirror.py:13, so hosts like attackerexample.com reach `c.get(url)` at mirror.py:16.
